video_notes.title: How to Systematically Setup LLM Evals (Metrics, Unit Tests, LLM-as-a-Judge)
video_notes.contributed: Not about front-end UI design at all — a crash course on evaluating LLM/agent applications (unit tests, human/LLM-judge alignment, A/B testing); contributes no citable UI-design claims to this guide.

video_notes.title: The Best AI Automation Stack to Learn in 2026
video_notes.contributed: Names the specific front-end stack (React + Vite + shadcn/ui) recommended for building AI-automation UIs, and frames the claim that AI has largely solved front-end coding while UX/design taste remains a human bottleneck.

video_notes.title: How I Build Insane Three.js Websites With Claude Opus 5
video_notes.contributed: A concrete AI-assisted design workflow for building striking Three.js/3D landing pages with Claude Code (Opus 5): reference-first prompting, MCP-driven inspiration gathering, effort-level settings, and turning repeatable techniques into reusable skills.

video_notes.title: Web Design for Beginners | FREE COURSE
video_notes.contributed: The only source that teaches manual UI/UX design fundamentals end-to-end — project briefs, wireframes, color theory, typography, the eight-point spacing system, common UI patterns (headers, heroes, buttons, galleries, footers, testimonials, tabs, accordions, forms), and responsive breakpoints — applied to a real Figma project.

claims.claim: A web designer is responsible for the entire front end (colors, typography, spacing, shapes, information architecture) while a web developer/engineer builds the back end — conflating the two roles causes client/professional friction.
claims.quote: in charge of designing the front end of a website

claims.claim: UX design is about understanding what users want and need and building a seamless experience around that (information architecture, usability testing, content strategy) — it is a distinct specialization from visual UI design.
claims.quote: understand what users want and what they need

claims.claim: UI design covers aspects that relate almost exclusively to a project's visual appearance — color, typography, spacing, sizing, shape — applied on top of the structure UX defines.
claims.quote: covers aspects that relate almost exclusively to the visual appearance

claims.claim: Every web design project should start with a written project brief (client background, site structure, content, design guidelines) before any color or typeface decision is made.
claims.quote: always start a web project with a brief

claims.claim: A wireframe is a low-fidelity sketch representing only content and structure — no color, no typography, no sizing decisions belong in it.
claims.quote: low-fidelity versions of your final design

claims.claim: A wireframe should be devoid of any intentional aesthetic decisions like color or typography so the UI designer isn't anchored to layout choices made before design begins.
claims.quote: devoid of any intentional aesthetic decisions like color or typography

claims.claim: Figma is the recommended UI design tool for beginners because it's free, cross-platform, and runs in the browser — Photoshop/Illustrator were not built for this workflow and should be avoided.
claims.quote: free, crossplatform, and works in the browser

claims.claim: A tint is created by mixing white into a color, a shade by mixing black, and a tone by mixing gray — these are the three core color-manipulation moves used to build a palette.
claims.quote: a tint is when you add white to a specific color

claims.claim: CMYK (subtractive) is for print; RGB and HSB (additive) are the color models used for screens/digital design.
claims.quote: CMYK stands for cyan, magenta, yellow, and black

claims.theme: Hex is the practical web format
claims.claim: Hexadecimal is the most popular color format in web design because it's a compact, easily shareable stand-in for RGB values.
claims.quote: the hex format is the most popular when it comes to web design

claims.claim: Blue is the single most-used color on the internet and conveys trust, calm, and security — which is why tech brands and financial institutions default to it.
claims.quote: the most used color on the internet, fun fact

claims.claim: Of all the color-harmony options in a tool like Adobe Color, analogous, monochromatic and complementary are the three used in practice most of the time.
claims.quote: monochromatic and complimentary are the most used

claims.theme: Never use pure black for text
claims.claim: Avoid pure black (#000) for body text — it contrasts too harshly; mix a primary-tinted gray instead.
claims.quote: against doing is to use pure black

claims.claim: Create a 'black' color that mixes a bit of the brand's primary hue with gray, then derive reusable tints (75/50/25/10/5%) for text, muted copy and separators instead of re-deriving grays each time.
claims.quote: mixing my primary hue with a bit of gray

claims.claim: Every text or interactive-element color must be checked for proper contrast against its background using a contrast-checker app before the palette is finalized — several of the tone-25/tone-10 tints will fail this check.
claims.quote: it has proper contrast compared to its background

claims.claim: As a beginner, source fonts from Google Fonts (free) or Adobe Fonts (paid, more granular filters by weight/width/x-height and higher perceived quality).
claims.quote: get your fonts from either Google Fonts or Adobe Fonts

claims.claim: Match typeface style to brand feeling: a serif as the big headline typeface signals luxury/sophistication, while sans-serif signals modern and trustworthy (why Stripe uses sans-serif, not serif).
claims.quote: go for a serif font as the big headliner

claims.claim: When using two typefaces, reserve the more-readable-at-small-sizes face for body text/buttons/menus/captions and the other for large headings.
claims.quote: the fonts with the greatest readability for smaller elements

claims.claim: Brandon Grotesque (headings) pairs well with Proxima Nova (body) — Proxima Nova stays legible at 16–18px where Brandon Grotesque does not.
claims.quote: pairs very well with Proximanova

claims.claim: Use a type-scale tool (typescale.com) with a chosen base font size (e.g. 21px for an airy, white-space-heavy design) to auto-generate the full heading scale.
claims.quote: use a base font size of 21 pixels

claims.claim: A 1.414 ('augmented fourth') ratio gives a good balance between small and large font-size contrast for a project scale.
claims.quote: an augmented fourth scale or 1.414

claims.claim: Every spacing/sizing dimension (margins, padding, widths, heights) should be a multiple of 8 — it's simple to remember, keeps measurements consistent across a project, and makes handoff to developers easier.
claims.quote: every dimension is basically a multiple of eight

claims.claim: Example applied padding: 16px top/bottom and 32px left/right on a button — both multiples of 8.
claims.quote: a padding of 16 pixels on top and bottom

claims.claim: Grid systems can add unnecessary complexity for beginner projects; a simpler ruler/guide-based alignment approach is often sufficient and easier to learn.
claims.quote: grids can add a certain degree of complexity to a project

claims.claim: Icons must share a consistent visual style (all outline or all solid) — mixing styles within one UI reads as sloppy even if icons come from different sets.
claims.quote: be consistent and use icons with the same style

claims.claim: Bootstrap Icons is a free, 1,600+ icon set worth defaulting to; Font Awesome, Heroicons (230 icons, MIT-licensed) and IconJar (icon-organizer app) are the other go-to resources.
claims.quote: over 1,600 icons. It's free to use

claims.claim: Prefer real client photos over stock photography wherever possible; reserve stock photos only for generic background context, never for 'people at work' cliché shots.
claims.quote: stay away from stock photos as much as possible

claims.claim: A header is the top section of a page and typically contains logo, nav menu, CTA and optionally a search field — but the structure is flexible (can go vertical, can hide nav under a menu button).
claims.quote: the top section of a web page that contains the logo

claims.claim: The hero area sits immediately below/next to the header, is 'prime real estate' because it's above the fold, and should carry the strongest message plus a CTA.
claims.quote: the area immediately below or next to the header

claims.claim: Buttons must be easy to click and to tap on mobile — size them for a finger, which is much larger than a cursor.
claims.quote: easy to click but also more importantly easy to tap

claims.claim: Every interactive button needs explicitly designed default, hover, active and disabled states, plus a subdued secondary style for lower-emphasis actions.
claims.quote: consider the different states that element can be in

claims.claim: Never use fake testimonials — it's both unethical and illegal; wait for real client feedback rather than fabricating quotes for a new business.
claims.quote: not use fake testimonials ever

claims.claim: Tabs show exactly one panel at a time; accordions can show multiple open panels simultaneously and suit simpler text content — which is why accordions dominate FAQ sections.
claims.quote: accordians can display multiple panels at once

claims.claim: A contact form needs only name, email address and message as the bare minimum — extra required fields (budget, company size, purpose) reduce completion rates.
claims.quote: all you need is their name, email address, and their message

claims.claim: Ethan Marcotte's 2010 List Apart article coined the term 'responsive web design'; it became the industry standard once media queries saw widespread adoption in 2012, replacing separate 'm.' mobile subdomains.
claims.quote: he named it responsive web design and this term stuck

claims.theme: Breakpoints should be discovered, not assumed
claims.claim: Relying on 'standard' fixed breakpoints (1024/768/480) is unreliable because different layouts break at different widths — instead, resize the canvas until a problem visibly appears and set the breakpoint there.
claims.quote: relying on those fixed break points is not ideal

claims.theme: Breakpoint ranges used on the demo project
claims.claim: The demo portfolio site used three empirically-found ranges: laptop >1200px, tablet 1200–600px, phone <600px, each with its own type scale and spacing.
claims.quote: phone range with screen sizes of less than 600 pixels

claims.claim: Major section spacing shrinks step-wise across breakpoints — 256px on large screens down to 168px on tablet and 96px on phone — so smaller screens aren't wasted on desktop-scale whitespace.
claims.quote: distance between each major section on large screens is 256

claims.claim: To make a tab-and-card component responsive, progressively strip repeated label text, shrink icon/padding values, stack cards two-per-row, then swap text labels for icons entirely at the smallest widths.
claims.quote: the easiest thing to do is make them

claims.claim: Before shipping a design to development, link screens together in Figma's prototype mode to simulate the user journey and catch navigation problems early.
claims.quote: an interactive mockup of your design that allows you

claims.claim: For AI-automation front ends, the recommended stack is React for components, Vite as the dev/build server, and shadcn/ui for pre-built components (buttons, graphs, chat UIs).
claims.quote: combination of three things that I recommend that is react, fight, and shet UI

claims.claim: shadcn/ui components are copied directly into your project's source rather than installed as a node_modules dependency, so both you and your coding agent can freely edit and restyle them.
claims.quote: you import that code into your project. So now it's there

claims.theme: AI has solved front-end code, not UX
claims.claim: AI can now build front-end code trivially, but there remains a real gap between just building a front end and doing actual UX/design work — AI still lacks in the latter.
claims.quote: difference between the actual exercise of creating the front end versus the design and the UX

claims.theme: AI has solved front-end code, not UX
claims.claim: The speaker's provocative claim: being 'just' a front-end developer with no other skills is no longer valuable because AI makes building simple front ends this easy.
claims.quote: just being a front-end developer, like you're cooked

claims.claim: Most AI-automation projects only need simple internal tools — admin dashboards and simple chat applications — not consumer-grade polished UX.
claims.quote: internal tools simple admin dashboards simple chat applications

claims.theme: File size as a quality signal
claims.claim: A fully 3D, interactive Three.js landing page (weather effects, animated towers, dynamic lighting) was built at under 1MB total file size — proof that visually rich sites don't require heavy asset payloads.
claims.quote: less than 1 meg in term of file size

claims.claim: 'AI slop' results from vague, unspecialized prompts — asking for 'a landing page' without a specific reference or vocabulary produces the same generic output every time.
claims.quote: you ask something too vague, and then you get something extremely standard

claims.claim: Connecting an MCP server like Mobbin lets the coding agent autonomously research and fetch high-quality UI reference examples (e.g. 'find the top UI for a mobile design for a travel app') instead of you manually browsing inspiration sites.
claims.quote: find the top UI for a mobile design for a travel app

claims.theme: Starter prompt for cloning a reference
claims.claim: The go-to starter prompt for a new AI-built landing page is simply pasting a reference URL and saying 'recreate this in a single HTML file. Self-verify until it's perfect' — no manual description of typography/layout needed anymore.
claims.quote: recreate this in a single HTML file. Self-verify until it's perfect

claims.theme: Reasoning effort matters for design quality
claims.claim: Always run the coding agent at maximum/'extra high' reasoning effort for front-end design work — medium effort produces noticeably worse, less-researched results.
claims.quote: auto is just enough. It's safer

claims.theme: Reasoning effort matters for design quality
claims.claim: Extra-high effort is described as the 'bare minimum' setting for getting non-slop design output from Opus 5 or Codex.
claims.quote: extra is my bare minimum here

claims.claim: Modern coding agents can use a tool like Playwright to scroll a reference site and record the interaction themselves, giving them frame-by-frame context on animations and scroll behavior that used to be impossible to convey in a text prompt.
claims.quote: use a tool like Playwright, do the scrolling for you

claims.claim: Getting a high-fidelity, non-slop AI-generated design costs meaningfully more in tokens, money and time than a quick generic prompt — the trade-off is explicit, not free.
claims.quote: yes, it will lose a lot of tokens

claims.claim: Cloning a reference design is only the starting point — the real design skill is developing enough vocabulary and taste to progressively mold the clone into something original and on-brand.
claims.quote: grow your vocabulary, your taste, your ability to

claims.claim: Ask the image model explicitly for transparent PNGs (rather than framed images) so elements can be layered and floated to create parallax depth effects — this is the same technique historically done manually in Figma layers.
claims.quote: you want to ask also is you want transparent PNG

claims.claim: canvasui.dev provides copy-paste shader-effect prompts (water, cloth, flame) that apply visual effects directly onto HTML elements rather than as a separate rendering layer.
claims.quote: shader effects on top of HTML

claims.claim: Once a technique (a texture pipeline, a weather effect, an orbit animation) works, capture it as an agent 'skill' so it can be reliably reused across future projects instead of re-prompted each time.
claims.quote: you want to tell your AI to turn that into skills

claims.theme: Super prompts capture an entire design
claims.claim: A 'super prompt' is a full text description distilled from a video/reference that captures the entire website design, letting you regenerate the same structure under a completely different brand/theme from a clean starting point.
claims.quote: the super prompt is going to describe the entire website

claims.claim: skills.sh is a directory for finding reusable agent skills, including a 'kill AI slop' family of skills specifically for stripping AI-sounding writing/design patterns.
claims.quote: really good for finding the skills, such as grill me

claims.claim: Open-sourcing finished AI-built projects builds an audience and functions as a portfolio — engineers historically used GitHub stars the way others used a personal website to attract hiring interest.
claims.quote: you will get the audience. You will get a portfolio

claims.claim: Once a base clone exists, ask the AI to generate multiple style/layout/copy options to prototype against before locking anything in permanently — don't settle for the first output.
claims.quote: gives you these options to prototype the design

disagreements.topic: How front-end UI work should actually get made

positions.position: UI design is a craft built from first principles — color theory, typographic scales, an eight-point spacing system, hand-built common patterns — executed manually in Figma over a 5+ hour course.

Modern practice is to paste a reference URL into an AI coding agent (Claude Opus 5) and let it replicate and self-verify the design; the human's job shifts to curating references and 'molding' the AI output rather than hand-building the layout system.

Being solely a hands-on front-end coder/builder is no longer valuable ('you're cooked') because AI has commoditized the build step — though this same video concedes AI still lacks genuine UX/design judgment.

disagreements.topic: How easy AI-driven front-end work actually is

positions.position: The AI/front-end layer for automation projects is framed as simple — most projects need only basic internal dashboards or chat UIs, and getting a working front end is comparatively trivial.

Achieving a genuinely non-slop, high-quality AI-generated design (like the Three.js showcase site) required running at maximum reasoning effort for 40+ minutes, high token spend, and iterative manual 'molding' — explicitly not fast or cheap.

gaps: No source covers accessibility beyond basic color-contrast checking — no guidance on ARIA, keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, or focus management.

No source explains how a finished Figma design or an AI-cloned reference actually gets translated into production HTML/CSS/component code, or what a design-to-dev handoff process looks like in practice.
No source compares component/design-system tooling beyond a single mention of shadcn/ui — no discussion of design tokens, Storybook, or maintaining a design system at scale.
No source discusses user testing, usability testing, or validating a UI design with real users before shipping.
No source gives any data connecting specific design decisions (color, layout, copy) to measurable business outcomes like conversion rate or engagement.
The AI-driven workflow videos (G-F5Qvy-7KM, omU3zR3K7-U) don't explain how to evaluate whether an AI-generated design is actually usable/accessible, only whether it looks distinctive ('non-slop').

No source covers motion/animation design principles systematically — the Three.js video shows effects (weather, cloth, orbiting) as anecdotal outcomes without a framework for when/how much motion to use.

No source addresses design work for non-marketing UI (e.g., dense data tables, enterprise dashboards, forms with complex validation) — B-ytMSuwbf8's patterns are all marketing/portfolio-site oriented.
